Question: Let \(f\) be a polynomial function such that, for all real \(x,\) \[ f(x^2+1)=x^4+5x^2+3. \] For all real \(x,\) \(f(x^2-1)\) is
Solution:
The input \(x^2+1\) suggests treating that entire expression as one variable. Every real \(t\ge1\) can be written as \(t=x^2+1\), by taking \(x=\sqrt{t-1}\). Hence the given equation yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(t)&=(t-1)^2+5(t-1)+3\\
&=t^2+3t-1
\end{aligned}
\]
for every \(t\ge1\).

We need this formula at inputs \(x^2-1\), which can be below \(1\). This is where the polynomial assumption matters. Define the polynomial
\[
g(t)=f(t)-(t^2+3t-1).
\]
It is zero for every \(t\ge1\), so it has infinitely many distinct zeros. A nonzero polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) distinct zeros: each zero supplies a linear factor, and factoring out distinct zeros successively lowers the degree by one each time. Thus \(g\) must be the zero polynomial, and \(f(t)=t^2+3t-1\) holds for every real \(t\).

We may therefore substitute \(t=x^2-1\) for any real \(x\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(x^2-1)
&=(x^2-1)^2+3(x^2-1)-1\\
&=x^4+x^2-3.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is choice B.
